selected.description: Richard Pococke (1704-1765) came from a prominent family. He studied at Cambridge, followed a career in the church and became a prelate. Pococke travelled in Europe (France, Italy, Germany, Austria, Poland, Hungary) together with his cousin from 1733 to 1736. In 1737, he set out on a tour of the East which lasted three years; starting from Egypt, he visited the Holy Land, Cyprus, Crete, the Aegean islands, Asia Minor and modern-day Continental and Northern Greece, the last two being territories hardly trodden by travellers at that time. Pococke travelled in Ireland in the years 1747-1760. From 1765 onwards he made various journeys in Britain as a bishop. ( Ioli Vingopoulou,  Aikaterini Laskaridis Foundation)

selected.title: Journal of the Resolution's voyage, in 1772, 1773, 1774, and 1775: On discovery to the southern hemisphere,... Also a journal of the Adventure's voyage, in the years 1772, 1773, and 1774.... Illustrated with a chart,... and other cuts. F. Newbery, at the corner of St. Paul's Church-Yard, 1775.
selected.description: [MARRA, John] Journal of the Resolution's Voyage, in 1772, 1773, 1774, and 1775. On Discovery to the southern hemisphere, by which the non existence of an undiscovered continent ... is demonstratively proved. Also a journal of the Adventure's voyage, in the years 1772, 1773, and 1774. With an account of the separation of the two ships London: 1775. Octavo. 1 folding engraved map, 5 engraved plates, extra-illustrated with 1 folding engraved map "Part of the Tropical Discoveries of the Resolution Sloop Captain J. Cook in 1774" Light dampstaining to a few leaves, some minor foxing. Modern paneled calf, gilt leather label "The first printed account of man's entry into the region south of the Antarctic circle" (Spence) and the earliest published complete account of Cook's second voyage, issued at least eighteen months prior to the official version. "A rare work ... contain[ing] details of many events not recorded in the official account, and a preface recording the causes which led Banks and his staff to withdraw from the expedition at the last moment. Accordingly it is a vital second voyage item..." (Davidson). The second voyage included the first crossing of the Antarctic circle, making Marra's narrative the earliest firsthand account of the Antarctic, and the engraved plates are the first depictions of that region. Due to the strict regulations against private publications, the work was published anonymously, but the identity of the author did not remain a mystery for long. "Correspondence between Cook and the Admiralty shows that the author was John Marra, one of the gunners' mates in the Resolution. He was an Irishman whom Cook had picked up at Batavia during the first voyage. He made an abortive attempt to desert at Tahiti on 14 May 1774, an escapade of which Cook took so lenient a view that he says - 'I know not if he might have obtained my consent, if he had applied for it in proper time.' This did not, however, as Marra states at p. 241, prevent his being put in irons..." (Holmes). This copy contains the extremely rare extra folded map, "Part of the Tropical Discoveries of the Resolution Sloop Captain J. Cook in 1774," which is noted by Beddie and Rosove, but which is not called for in most of the references. This map has been present in only three of the twenty-five copies of the first edition sold at auction in the last thirty or so years. The chart appears opposite the first page of text and shows New Caledonia and the Great Cyclades islands to the north and Norfolk island to the south. It is a most interesting production, and is to be found in two states: first, as here with the engraver's name and with the position of Norfolk Island incorrectly placed 4° too far south; and second, with the engraver's name erased (but just visible), with Norfolk Island's latitude corrected. The chart follows two of the Gilbert manuscript charts (see David 2.225/6/) in spelling Ballabeah Isle with a final "h," unlike all the other manuscript charts. We have a definite date for the corrected issue of this chart, as it accompanied the article, "Late Voyages of the Resolution and Adventure," published in the Gentleman's Magazine, Vol. XLVI, 1776 (edited by David Henry), opposite page 120 in the March issue. Therefore, it seems probable that the uncorrected chart found its way into copies of Marra issued during the last two or three months of 1775. selected.title: Travel journal from Italy to the Middle East
description: Antiquariat Inlibris Gilhofer Nfg. GmbH;

The manuscript is neatly handwritten in French in brown ink. It consists of 60 unnumbered pages of text and is illustrated with several drawings of floor plans and elevations of church buildings and details of architectural decorations executed in pencil and pen, and ink drawings of coins

This anonymous seventeenth-century account of a trip from Rome to Jerusalem and Egypt begins with a glossary of Neapolitan terms, followed by two pages of detailed renderings of coins from Naples and Malta. After these preliminaries the account of the voyage begins with departure from Rome on 21 December 1666. The description of Naples includes an account of the antiquities of Pozzuoli, which the traveler visits on 4 January 1667 while waiting for a favorable wind to speed him to Sicily. Having reached the island, he departs from Messina on February 19th for Malta. The description of Malta includes numerous ink sketches of monuments and views shaded in pencil. Sailing from Malta on March 16th, the traveler stops at the Cyclades, Rhodes, and Cyprus before reaching Tyre in Lebanon. Following the coast of the Mediterranean Sea southwards, he visits Acre and Jaffa, then sets out for the holy sites of Palestine. Five full-page pencil illustrations include the skyline of Jerusalem, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Mount Olive, and a three-dimensional plan of the Via Dolorosa. The traveler departs Jerusalem on June 16th and continues his trip towards Egypt. After arriving in Damietta, he seeks out the French consul in Cairo, then takes a tour of the pyramids. Also, he witnesses the splendid entry of the Pacha of Baghdad into Cairo and gives a detailed account of the pomp arranged for the Pacha's reception in the city. He embarks then for Alexandria where he describes the St. Mark's Coptic Cathedral; then sails for Crete and, after more adventures, returns to the south of France, and from there, on horseback, to Rome. The final leaf, in the same hand, contains an Italian key to a map of Jerusalem
The text contains several small corrections and revisions by the author, perhaps evidence of the manuscript being composed and illustrated during the journey

Inlibris acquired this work at auction in the UK (Dominic Winter, sale 15 May 2013, lot 265); it has previously been in a private UK collection for more then 50 years. Formerly in the Gloucester City Libraries, with their old ownership and withdrawal stamp on endpapers at front and rear

selected.description: A general history of the Aphrodite of Milos (Venus de Milo). The author wrote the book with Greek readers in mind. The author's stated purpose was to methodically compare accounts and eyewitness stories to find the truth about the discovery of the statue, and what happened to the statue subsequently. A quick history of the island of Milos, a small number of illustrations and two maps are included. A few pages are legible but slightly blurry in the gutters due to scanning. There is some Greek handwriting in a few spots (notes)?

selected.title: ON THE ROAD - A Coruna / Dakar
selected.description: ON THE ROAD -  A Coru ña / Dakar So, I’m leaving A Coruña, a city placed on the top-west corner of Spain, Galicia department. Actually walking along the Fernando Suárez García avenue now, an avenue just in front of the sea, by the left side of the Orzán cove, that the Greco-Roman geographers designated as Portus Magnus Artabrorum. being the Artabri, I got to know, an ancient Gallaeci-Celtic tribe that used to dwell around this lands. And so, as I walk by the Paseo Maritimo, I’m actually contemplating the imposing masses of granite rocks that rise against the harshness of the sea. And, with very fresh winds blowing against my face, I actually pass by the “Miradoiro Fiestra ó Atlántico”, that lays just in front of three small islets, Illa Vendaval, Illa do Pé, and Illa Aguión. Further, I’m actually going around a small and sympathetic cove that form the Portiño harbor, also called “Porto de San Pedro de Visma”, being Visma the name of the neighborhood here, and well, as it goes, I’m now passing right on the side of the Miradoiro do Faroleiro (Lighthouse Keeper's viewpoint), following along the Punta do Burro (donkey's tip), soon reaching Suevos, a small hamlet that is part of the Arteixo municipality, named like this after the Suevi, a group of Germanic peoples that migrated from central Europe to this area during the “barbarian” invasions of the fifth century, I got to know. Then, after exchanging some impressions with the villagers I meet on the street, in front of houses with unpainted walls. I’m leaving this humble hamlet on the top of the hill, coming back to the seaside, already going along the “soap beach” or “Praia de Sabón”, getting close to Malpica, a place indicated as the starting point of the so-called “death coast”, known for its high cliffs and severe weather, located near the  Sisargas Islands , a notoriously dangerous, rocky spot where numerous ships have sunk… I got to know. And so, as I walk by this piece of coast, I pass by the Beo beach, the Seiruga beach, the Barizo beach, the Punta Nariga lighthouse, then going along a narrow dirt path through lush, low-lying vegetation, always by the sea, I end up reaching the Areia de Prata beach, plus the Niñóns and the Morro beach. Afterwards, as I come back to the road, I will pass Brantuas de Arriba, Casas da Espereira, Brantuas de Abaixo, As Gurichas, Carballido, A Brixéria, Cospindo, Carracido, Cedeira, Ponteso, between others... I go though the bridge over the Allones river, and I keep following along the AC429 national road, not hitchhiking, just walking fast. And so, after having passed Sinde, Borneiro, As Pias, Reparada, Vimianzo, Vilaseco, Berdeogas, Bustelo, Lobelos, and Sardiñeiro de Abaixo, I reach the so colled lobster cove and then, finally, the Cape Finisterre, that ages ago was appointed as “the world’s end”, this is, it is here, at this rocky beach, that I end up meeting with some pilgrims coming from the many corners of Europe, and say, as I’m already approaching some of these people here around this fire, I realize what they are actually doing right now… this is, some of them are actually burning their socks, spreading the smoke and the smell around, laughing while doing it, and… as it goes, throwing these same burnt socks down the cliffs by the sea… Thus, while watching them, I wish I could do the same, but no, because, actually, I’m not wearing any socks… so, I have this idea, instead of socks, I end up burning my shoes, and then yes, like them, I’m throwing my burnt snikas down the cliffs by the sea… and so, in the meanwhile, after exchanging some words with a few of those pilgrims here wandering around the fire, I get to know that most of them are actually coming from Eastern Europe, but, not only that, there are also a couple of them coming from that countries on the strip of land between Europe and Asia, this is, the so-called middle-east, and well, after getting to know about the reasons that impelled them to come here, nothing religious, I may say, we all get into some kind of singing, and further… as I see some of them actually playing castanets while doing some dancing moves, I also start to rummage inside my rucksack, and from there picking my small harmonica that instantly I start to blow while actually washing my feet on the sea. And say, after much playing and dancing around this rugged rocks, some of us become acquainted, share stories, divide in small groups, and in a while, me and my group are already walking in the direction of Santiago de Compostela, a city about fifty miles from here, to the east… and so, once there, as we go through this clerical city, soon we get to understand how the locals are actually tired of all this shabby pilgrims coming here to spread their misery around, people in the search of miracles, others, just mere tourists, interested in photographing the misery of the others… and, as we get to the “plaza del Obradoiro”, the main plaza in front of the main cathedral, my escorts disappear, and I go to explore the city alone, this is, I get to hear some conversations from the locals, and also, I meet some other travelers, and again, I get to hear stories about how they actually got here, and in the meanwhile there I go, setting myself  under a porch, playing the harmonica, I mean, busking… this is, right now clusters of people are actually passing by in front of me, groping through the haze, some looking at me with indignation, this while the bells from the adjacent cathedrals clatter, as thus, as they clatter, I’m actually trying to play in their rhythm… this is, time passes by, and when night is already coming, I see two strange dudes getting close, one thinner, the other fatter, smiling and smirking, exchanging whispered comments between them while approaching... And so, at some point, the thinner one is already offering me loose wine, while the other, the chubbier one, just sits down on the floor on my side and begins ordering people to get closer and give money to the player (me). This is, in a while, they are both saying nonsense things in a pretentious semi-operatic tone, and eventually, at some point, the thinner one even starts doing some dancing steps, with one hand on the chest, and the other, the bustier one, here he is now, rolling on the floor at our front, tying up the passers-by, and laughing non-stop while doing so. And well, as it goes, the gaunt faced one is already giving me orders, telling me to play it slower and simpler, say, telling me to play only the bass notes, to do like a waltz rhythm, and, accordingly, as I do it, here he comes, already asking me pointless questions, and then singing with some kind of operatic style, well, not really operatic but… while the other, the chubbier one, that before was sitting on the floor, is now calling “Vaca Loca” to anyone that passes by our side, and then, immediately, offering the neck of his bottle to whoever deposits coins inside the hat at our front. And so, at this point, the gaunt faced one, is actually singing about “damas desnudas con bigotes de harina...”; “filipoyas místicos…”; “piruletas macabras…” and other things I can’t really understand, coz his language sounds like Russian. And then, just then, when the wine is finished and his voice begins to fail, I see them confiding something between themselves in my back, and so, as a result of this, in a while, I’m actually being invited to leave this place and accompany them somewhere, this is, they need a driver, the gaunt faced one tells me. And promptly, without knowing about directions, I accept to be their driver, thus, after collection the coins from that hat set on the floor here in front of us... there we go, already leaving this place, but, as we try to advance, the chubbier one doesn’t want to move, and then, when he tries to move, actually, he keeps going against walls and stuff, even falling on the floor a couple of times, this because he is dead drunk, so, both of us have to supporting him on the move, bracing him both sides, so he doesn't fall to the ground again. And thus, while we pull him, actually, he continues to snort words, things that are incomprehensible, this while his friend keeps pulling him, giving him shoves, offering him a beating, a scene that is somehow comic and depressing at the same time. And therefore, in those ways we wandering through the city, actually looking for the place they have parked their car… and, while advancing, the chubbier one, despite being almost in a sleeping mode, when he opens his eyes, he is still howling, calling dirty names to anyone that crosses our sight. And then, finally, when we manage to find the car, a Rover GSI, that actually was parked inside some public garden, a garden adjacent to some kind of semi-rotten church, we throw the paunchy one onto the back seat, and there we go, seating on the front, me on the driver’s seat, and the gaunt face, his name Alberto, on my side… this is, is not easy to maneuver the car out of this park, but when I manage to do it... following the hints of Alberto, I’m already getting on the AP-9, say, a motorway heading towards Pontevedra, and as it goes, with my co-pilot getting asleep, and the one in the back already snoring, after passing Vigo and Ó Porriño, I’m actually driving towards the Portuguese border, because those were the instructions Alberto gave me. And so, accordingly, as we pass the border, I have to wake him up again, because I need to know about directions… And so, as we pass Valença, the first town in Portuguese lands, Alberto (half asleep), order me new directions, and so, there we go, following along some national road and then an earthy path, and well, at some point, after having passed some pine tree forests, we are actually reaching some kind of farm with a few adjacent shacks, and at this point I understand, this place here is actually some kind blacksmith workshop, and so, following his instructions, I do park the car somewhere, and well, by now, as I try to get out of the car, instantly, I get surrounded by huge dogs that do not look very friendly, but, instantly, as its owner (Alberto) shouts at them, they back off. And so, at this point, as we make our way out of the car, leaving the paunchy one there snoring in the back seat… there we go, already getting inside some of the adjacent shacks, say, entering some kind of kitchen that looks more a box room, and, as we move around, the man just approaches some wood barrel, opens the tap and fills two glasses with that liquid, this is, “now you can drink, finally...” he says, then adding, “this is a different kind from the ones you may have tasted in Santiago, I mean, it’s home-made green wine… ‘maduro’ we say, green but mature… and so, after all this talking, I want to try it… and oh boy, it’s really good, not acid like the one I have tried in Spain... I mean, really fruity, and then I’m ready to leave this place… thus, after piercing through the scattered pieces of scrap metal and wood lying about the front-yard, I come back to the road, and, while imagining being pursued by a bunch angry dogs, I run all night, just stopping at the sun rise, by the entrance of some village, this is, here I’m, seated inside some bus-stop shed, and, I still have time to sleep a couple of hours, this before some kids arrive, kids that are actually coming to get on the bus that will take them to the school placed on bigger city in the surroundings… this is, Braga city, the third bigger city in this country in terms of population, they say. And so, as the bus comes by, I quickly move to the last seat, and, despite the cackling that circles me, I permit myself to sleep a bit more… just opening my eyes when we get to the last station, this is, the bus station at the city center… and so, as I get out of this station, and randomly follow some streets, watching the people, I end up in front of some kind of castle, at a colorful garden, with some kind of romantic fountain in the middle, and thus, by this fountain I rest for a while, but, it’s early, so, not much people are coming into this garden, just a couple of youngs are crossing it, from time to time, and then, at some point, a homeless guy actually approaches me and asks for a cigarette, and so, I give him a stone that I had in my pocket, and, while staring at this stone, he starts to tell me the story of “Santa Barbara”, the patron saint of this garden and the castle on our back, this is, he says that “...in Vila Real, a city about one hundred kilometers from here, to the east, there lived a rich and powerful man who wanted to arrange a marriage for his daughter, Barbara, but the many suitors that he would bring to her, she would refuse, and so, he locked her in the tower of a castle, thus, making her unable to meet anyone of her interest, and then, one day, suspecting that some her suitors were actually entering through some kind of window that she herself had ordered to be opened in the this tower, her father, he himself, tried to kill her, but at the exact point that he was about to do so, a lightning came down from the sky and incinerated the man, being for this reason now, Santa Barbara, the patron saint of heavy artillery members, firefighters and miners who place their faith in this saint to protect themselves from unexpected explosions…” he says, and then, after hearing this fantastic explanation, this same man just accompany me until the surroundings of the train station, from where the motorway going in the southern direction departs, and as it goes, I quickly get a ride with some guy driving a Fiat Punto, actually driving in the direction of Oporto city, that is the place where I wanna go, and, because he works at some kind of laboratory, all the way we speak about virus and viruses, starting by the Escherichia coli, “also known as E. Coli,  a gram-negative, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped, coliform bacteria of the genus Escherichia that is commonly found in the lower intestine of warm-blooded organisms”, he says. And accordingly, about thirty minutes after, I’m already in Porto city, this is, at Boavista Square, some kind of roundabout on the north branch of the city... and so, as I ask directions people point me in a certain way, and soon I’m actually advancing through stone paved roads that lead me to the small Cedofeita church, a church with more than one thousand years, some locals say, and they also say that this church as actually some kind of municipality house from the Suebi, the Germanic people that I heard about in A Coruna. And then, after some small conversations about the Suebi and other Germanic tribes from that time, like the Marcomanni, the Quadi, the Hermunduri, the Semnones, and the Lombards, I go through the Cedofeita street, a pedestrian street that gives me the impression that I’m actually in Napoli, I don’t know why. And further, as I reach the main historic building from this city, the Clérigos Tower, a building with about three hundred years, that was a construction ordered by the “Clérigos Pobres Brotherhood”, a brotherhood that was a merger of three pre-existing brotherhoods that developed in the Santa Casa da Misericórdia do Porto, this is, the Brotherhood of São Pedro ad Vincula, the Congregation of São Filipe Néri and the Confraternity of Our Lady of Mercy. And so, I get to know, after the merger, the name of the brotherhood became “Confraria de Nossa Senhora da Misericórdia, São Pedro e São Filipe Néri”, later simplified as “Brotherhood of Clérigos”. And I also get to know that, the new brotherhood, intending to have its own headquarters, soon tried to achieve this objective, and when, in the beginning of the eighteenth century, they were offered land in the this so-called place of Cruz de Cassoa, next to the Adro dos Enforcados (a plot of land already outside the Fernandina Walls, near Olival, olive tree field, where criminals sentenced to hang and those who died outside of religion were buried), it was here, not without some controversy, that the house and Clérigos Tower would be built. And so, now, as I go down the Clérigos street, soon I reach the “praça da liberdade” or the “liberty square” at the bottom of “Aliados street” where is a monument to Dom Pedro IV, that at the same time as also Dom Pedro I, the first emperor of Brazil. And then, after turning right in front of the São Bento train station, I pass a series of terraces with skewed tables, and people sitting in a weird way, a place that, again, gives me the impression that I’m actually in Napoli, and continuing, as I go down a narrow pedestrian street called “Rua das Flores”, this is, “Flowers street”, instantly, some gypsy guys come to me offering cocaine and axixe, and, as I refuse it, one of guys even explains me that, the “tripas à moda do porto” dish is actually made from the muscle wall of a cow's stomach chambers, and “not from the intestines”, as some say, he says. And then, as I keep going down this “Rua das flores”, I appreciate the buildings with their tiled facades, some of them in semi-ruin, but still, with their lush pots of flowers up there, on the narrow verandas on the third or fifth floors. And then, after passing a couple of souvenir shops (actually owned by Indian dudes), I see, under some kind of porch, seated on the floor, a cadaveric man under a big umbrella,  talking bullshit to the passersby, this is, some kind of junkie, injecting his body in front of everybody, and so, I think to myself, definitely some kind of modern days Diogenes. And further, after leaving him alone, I pass some more buildings that look shutdown, but actually I see people getting in and out through that doors, and they are actually speaking foreign languages. And then, as I keep advancing, I come to approach this girl with an old fashioned bicycle on her side, the bicycle actually all covered with small drawings of paisajes, aquarelles, and so, at the first look, I get interested in one of her drawings, say, a drawing with a man in a trench coat, actually launching a large paper airplane into the air. And I also like his hat, coz, it looks like a postman from the old times. And, as I say this to her, straight away, she decides to offer me the drawing, and in exchange, I also offer her some stones I have in my pockets. And then, further, as I keep going down, I see a guy announcing lottery tickets, a woman selling crochet clothes, and then, as I pass a couple of restaurants with their tables in the middle of the street, and all the ones seated on these tables are tourists, and some more abandoned buildings on both sides of this street, buildings also covered with bluish mosaics, and on the ground floor, between the rusty pillars, there are some antique dealers, antique dealers that also sell costume jewelry, and then, as I get to the bottom of this street, I pass some kind of church with sea monsters coming out of its facade, and also, in front of the small entrance hall of this barricaded church, I see a brunette guy seated on the steps of this same church, not young not old, and, as I seat on his side, “my name is Fred”, he says, and when I ask him from where he’s from, “I’m Brazilian”, he says, and then, “but during the first years I lived in in this country, I lived in Lisbon, not here… but then… I traveled a bit through all western Europe… this is, I went to Spain, France, Italy and even Germany, where I stayed for a while, but that snow, man! That cold! I got depressed, I got sick, and in the end… it wasn't easy to come back. I mean, it wasn’t easy at all, but when I finally managed to do it, I ended up here, and so, I decided to make my base here, instead of Lisbon, which has already too many Brazilians…”, And, after hearing this, I also decide to say something about Berlin, but it looks that he’s not listening now, instead, he starts to hit the steps from the stairs where we are, this to show me that he is a drummer, and me, without wasting time, I also have something to show him, so yeah, there we go, both with the asses up and the arms down hammering this stony staircase with the palms, say, producing what can be called an impromptu drum battle. And, well, as it goes, after a while we are already being surrounded by a bunch of tourists and curious people taking photos of the situation, but then, we kick them out and move away. So, this is, as it goes, we move to Ribeira, really downtown, an area by the river, the Douro river, and so, on the way we buy a couple of wine bottles, and then, while we walk by the river, we pass some stalls with embroidered fabrics, handmade jewelry, etc. And just then, when we get close to that double decked bridge, the so-called “Don Luís” bridge, we go down by the water, and, as we go he actually presents me to some of his friends actually living here in barracks under the bridge... and so, in a while, we are already sharing drinks with them, and they, they also share some of their drinks with us, and then, there they go, inside their tents, then coming back with a bunch of percussive items like, djambês, timpanis, snare-drums, many kinds of tambourines, cymbals, pumpkin-shakers and other kinds of shakers, and so, there we go now, more and more close to the water, playing all this percussive stuff all night long. And so, just next morning I actually go across that bridge, say, when coming to the end of this bridge, I turn right, and while walking by the river on the other side, I actually pass by a bunch of Port wine cellars, this is, I pass brands like “Cockburn's”; “Taylor's”; “Cálem”; “Burmester”; “Sandeman”; “Ramos Pinto”; “Graham`s”; “Ferreira”; etc. And so, in the meantime, after having passed some ruins, a shipyard, some buildings under construction, and a series of abandoned lots, I’m actually by the sea, at the southern mouth of Douro river, in a place with some kind of dunes, and some bones buried there among the shards, and as it goes, the tide is actually rising and falling, quickly and then slowly, without rhythm, treacherous. And, as it goes, after reaching the Lavadores neighborhood, I go in search of the national road by the coast, going south, and accordingly, when I find it, there I stand at an intersection, showing up my thumb. And so, being taken by this and that car, I actually pass cities like Espinho, Esmoriz, Santa Maria da Feira, Ovar, Aveiro. Figueira da Foz, Nazaré, Peniche and Mafra, and well… soon I'm already going through the April’s bridge that goes over Tejo river, the river that separates Lisbon from Almada, or Al-ma'adan, “the mine”, and say, at this point, I’m actually being taken by a former university teacher, currently talking about Dona Urraca, apparently, the daughter of the first king of Portugal, he says, “Urraca was born in Coimbra in one thousand one hundred forty eight, and, she was the daughter of Afonso I, the first king of Portugal, and Maud of Savoy, the second or third daughter of Amadeus III, Count of Savoy and Maurienne, and Mahaut of Albon, the sister of Guigues IV of Albon, applied ‘le Dauphin’... and, one of her aunts, Adelaide of Maurienne, was actually the queen consort as the wife of King Louis VI of France, and one of her great-grand-uncles was Pope Callixtus II… and so, coming back to Dona Urraca, she actually married Ferdinand II of León, but, the marriage would be annulled about ten years after, coz, it was discovered, they were direct cousins, great-grandchildren of Alfonso VI of León and Castile…” and as he tells this things about the beginning of Portugal, and its connections with Spain, we actually pass towns like Laranjeiro, Corroios, Amora, Coina, Palmela, Marateca, Palma, Alcacer do Sal, “one of the most ancient cities in Europe, founded by Phoenician hairs, and apparently… it provided salt, salted fish, horses for export and food for the ships that traded with Cornwall, a ceremonial county in South West England… but, later, would be invaded by the Arabs, and it would become the capital of the of the Al-Kassr province…under the Umayyad rule of Damascus… this is, after an internal victory over Muwallad rebels in 888, a Moorish fleet transported troops from Alcácer to Oporto, to support Al-Mansur Ibn Abi Aamir, that culminated in the destruction of the sanctuary of Santiago de Compostela, in Galicia, northwest Spain..” he says. And so, as we keep talking about the time when the Arabs ruled over what is now Portugal and Spain, we pass Ervideira, Grandola, Santa Margarida da Serra, Roncão, Santiago do Cacem, Barbuda, and then, as we drive on the side of Sines, a coastal city on the Alentejo region, he just says, “This city holds an important oil refinery and… it is also the birthplace of Vasco da Gama,  the 1st Count of Vidigueira, a Portuguese explorer and nobleman that was, it is said, the first European to reach India by sea…”. And so, then, as I wander through the city, they tell me that this city hosts an important folk music festival, simply named, Festival de Musicas do Mundo de Sines, where already played names like Shemekia Copeland, Omar Sosa, Taraf de Haïdouks, Black Uhuru, Sly & Robbie, Hedningarna, Tinariwen, Sa Dingding, Kronos Quartet, The Skatalites, Lee "Scratch" Perry, Tom Zé, Femi Kuti, Hermeto Pascoal, Marc Ribot, Master Musicians of Jajouka, Señor Coconut, Trilok Gurtu, Toumani Diabaté, Rabih Abou-Khalil, Mahmoud Ahmed, Salif Keita, Gogol Bordello, Seun Kuti, Nortec Collective and Alamaailman Vasarat, etc. “Oh, the Master Musicians of Jajouka, that is great, I love them…” I say. And then, as they tell me that the best beaches in this country are actually between this city and Sagres, a city on the southwest tip of Portugal, this name tells me something, yes, I have seen it before a lot of times, because yes, Sagres is also the name of a famouse beer brand in this country… And so, as I go down the Costa Vicentina, I pass wonderful depopulated beaches with excavated cellars made inside schist-greywacke sedimentary kind of  rocks, and birds coming from Africa, like the swallow and the black stork, or Ciconia nigra, that, as I get to know, “all years travels between central African countries, like Burkina Faso, Niger, and south Portugal…” a fisherman tells me. And as it goes, after crossing several cliffs, walking up and down roads between beaches and pine forests with sandy terrains, at some point, I would eventually reach the southernmost part of the country, this is, Algarve, and so, as I go though it, I get to know that this name Al-Garbe, simply means “the west” in Arabic language, and so, at some point, when I’m crossing Albufeira, a city famous for being a hub of many English expats, I get in a van with a guy with a goatee and a ponytail, his name Yan. And soon, I got to know that he is actually transporter, this is, “I transport staff between south Portugal and south Spain and the opposite…” he says. And so, along the way, he would confide about his roots… “Say, actually I’m the son of an unscrupulous Englishman of lost whereabouts and a sketchy Greek woman, I mean… my childhood was spent in different islands of the Aegean Sea, where my parents met and lived for a while… inlands like Corfu, Milos, Nexus,  Amorgos, Ikaria, Rhodes, Lesbos, etc… this is, in these islands I had contact with the many fugitives from the Asian world, say Turks, Arabs, and other Middle Eastern creatures… and so, still young, I got into problems related with these acquaintances… and, at a certain point, my father sent me to an aunt in Italy, and then another one in France, but I hated France, so, I ended up with my paternal grandparents in Yorkshire, where I spent part of my adolescence… this is, I did some schooling there and then, I would found myself on the road again with a group of hippie bastards… this is, with them I went from Europe to Russia, and then from Kazakhstan to Uzbekistan, from Tajikistan to India, and then, we would hit Bangladesh, Myanmar, and finally Thailand… and so, in the meanwhile, my would friends leave, and I would move to Hong-Kong, where I would work for a while… and then, with the money I did there, I would take a flight to the States, this is, I traveled across America, I mean, I hitchhiked from Washington to Texas and Miami, and then, I even ended up living in the Caribbeans, for a while…” he says, as we pass the border, and then the coastal cities of Cadis, Mazagón, Matalascañas, and the Parque Nacional de Doñana, an area of marshes, shallow streams, and sand dunes in the delta where the Guadalquivir River flows into the Atlantic Ocean. And so, once we reach Gibraltar,  a city located at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula,  I even help him to unload some furniture here and there, and then, as he keeps his travel, there I stay, this is, in this enclaved British city, I discover a great tunnel perfect for busking, located really in the city center,  and so, during some days I would play my harmonica there, this while watching the tourists passing by, tourist from all europe and some from the Maghreb world also. And so, in the intervals of time between my playing and my moments of wandering, I would attend some morocco-style cafes, humble places that greatly differ from all the other British style kind of thing, where old Maghrebean men come to drink shay and smoke big cigarettes, this, while having their exalted conversations in Arab, Darija or Llanito, a form of Andalusian Spanish heavily laced with English and some arabesque expressions. And so, here I’m now, more precisely at “Roxy”, one of that places, this is, here I stay with Amin, and as it goes, say, while we smoke some pot, eventually, he decides to explain to me how he has actually crossed the Baḥr al-Maghrib,  this is, the Mediterranean sea, and so, here he goes now, already asserting that, “The first time we did it… we actually did it in a small dinghy made of inner tubes from truck wheels, you see, ‘kasdi’, and it happened that, the sea… actually dragged us to where we did not expect, and so, unintentionally, we ended up landing in south Portugal… this is, as we landed in Algarve, straight away my friends left to Spain, leaving me alone there… and so, in the meanwhile, I would go to Lisbon, where I would remain for some time, coz, I may say… I liked the Portuguese people, they are humbler than the Spanish, but… there aren't many work opportunities in that country, and so, after a while, I would leave the big city and go to work illegally in the extensive orange tree farms of southern Spain, mainly located around Valencia, say, a city that actually have ferries to the famous island of Ibiza, ‘kasdi’, and, attracted by this name… somehow, I managed to get into one of that ferrie, illegally, but, unfortunately or fortunately, I don’t know now, I got caught on the arrival and they sent me to a special kind of prison for illegals that turned out to be a forced labor camp, and so, there there was also people from Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and also some sub-sahariens, this is, people from Mali, Niger, Chad etc. And so, it was there that I learned how to properly speak and write is Spanish, and then, just then, when I already could speak and write in that language, they would send me back to Morocco… this is, my mother was happy to see me again, but I can’t say the same about my older brother, that soon would put me out of the house, this because, as he said, I had become an infidel... and so, I wandered through the country and eventually would end up in Ouarzazate, at the doors of the Sahara, on the side of the Barrage el Mansour Eddahbi, where I worked for a while, this before reaching Merzouga, a city on the border with Algeria… but you know, ‘kasdi’, in the desert there are no borders and so… after a while I would actually find myself in Tunis where I heard about a place people could cross into Europe, ‘kasdi’, and so... once again I got into a dinghy that would take me to Malta, a European island I had never heard about… say, an island where people speak Arab, Italian and French, all mixed up… and so, then, some months after I would actually reach Sicily, where I would for the Mafia, say, I would do numerous trips between Palermo and Napoli, and then, between Napoli and France, and so, that’s how I came to live in Montpelier and then in Marseille, but there, in Marseille, I got into a series of problems with some Algerian guys, this is, I got arrested, found illegal, and again, they sent back to my country… this is, my mother was happy to see me again, but not my brothers, the same as before… and so, after some months I would came back to Europe again, but, this time I would go to German, and then I would travel through some Balkan countries like Hungary, Serbia and Romania, and at some point, I would eventually reach Istanbul, in Turkey, this is, I would get some girlfriend there, and with her I would travel to Lebanon, where we separated, and then,  I would come back my country going all around the Baḥr al-Maghrib, this is, the Mediterranean sea, I mean, I would go through the occupied Palestinian territories, I would get a job in the port of Alexandria, in north Egypt, and so, after some time there, eventually, I would get in contact with the vessels transporting products between Egypt and other North African countries, and so… that’s how I managed to get back to my country...”, he says. And then, further, I'm no more in Gibraltar, this is, now I’m on the other side of the sea, in Tangier, more precisely, at the Grand Socco, a piazza at the top of one of the city's central hills, more precisely, an intersection of rue de la Plage with rue d'Italie with avenue Sidi Bou Arraquia with rue Sidi Bouabid with rue d'Angleterre and with rue de la Liberté, where there is a night market, and so, here I’m, now inspecting some old trinkets displayed on the cobbled floor around some kind of broken fountain, and so, as it goes, in the meanwhile, I even meet a group of young French people on their way to the Gnaowa music Festival, a festival taking place in the southern part of the country, more precisely Essaouira, former Mogador. Accordingly, I join the caravan, this is, I take the road with then in the direction of Essaouira, and so, going by the Atlantic coast, we pass Rabat, Casablanca, Safi, and then, I’m already at the camping area of the festival, in ‘Saouira, where I manage to make friendship with a couple of krakeb players, being the krakeb a large iron castanet-like thing that commands the rhythmic aspects of Gnawa music. And so, after some days there, attending jam sessions between Europeans, Arabs and Africans, roughly speaking, this people from the festival would take me to Agadir, and then to the Aglou Plage, that is already part of the Souss-Massa-Drâa... and then to Mirleft, perched on top of the gigantic ocher-colored cliffs, where I would eventually find locals selling pots of argan oil, and then Sidi Ifni and Tan-Tan, a town already surrounded by the desert and further, on the border with the Western Sahara, some guy driving a very old Mercedes Benz would actually take me to the  springs of the Layoun oasis, springs that furnish Laayoune, the capital of the western Sahara, and then, the driver of another truck with a load of pumpkins, would eventually give me a ride until the border with Mauritania... and afterwards, a group of Touaregs would actually take me to the vicinities of Dakar. And so, this is, here I’m now, at Malika beach, just on the side of some fish cottages where there are some pirogues turned upside down, pirogues with sentences saying things like “Papa Alada Ndao”; “Yeye Fatow”; “Dieng Dieng Dieng”; “Noo Ko Bokk”, etc. And then, as I wander around, a fisherman that is also a kora player, would eventually accompany me to the city center of Dakar, and so, this is, now, I’m already reaching the Boulevard Dial Diop, and then, as it goes, I pass the Place de l'Obélisque, I go down Boulevard du General de Gaulle that takes me to the Medina where I meet someone that actually wants buy my hair, and then, after passing the Our Lady of Victories monument, I go down Av. Pasteur, I pass the Ancien palais de Justice, now converted into an improvised art center, and finally, well, finally I arrive at Cap Manuel, a place that is said to be the westernmost point of Africa, and so, here I stay, just in front of the Atlantic sea, imagining what can be there, on the other side.

selected.title: A stain in the blood : the remarkable voyage of Sir Kenelm Digby : pirate and poet, courtier and cook, king's servant and traitor's son
description: xix, 553 pages : 24 cm

On 16 August 1628, five battle-scarred English ships sailed through the narrow entrance of the harbour on the Greek island of Milos. Dropping anchor, the 25-year old captain banqueted with the local lord before sitting down to write an account of his journey - an account that would transform him entirely. Sir Kenelm Digby was known as one of the most extraordinary Englishmen who ever lived: a trusted advisor to the King, a pioneering philosopher and scientist, a friend and patron to Ben Jonson, Thomas Hobbes and van Dyck, and a thinker whose ideas are as relevant now as they were during his own troubled times. He was also widely known as the 'son of a traytor and husband of a whore': a man who witnessed his father's gruesome execution for high treason, and the lover of the most celebrated beauty of the age, Venetia Stanley. In an attempt to clear his name, and on a quest for personal glory, Digby assembled a fleet and set sail for the Mediterranean. His journey - encompassing fevers, mutiny, piracy, daring rescues and heroic sea battles - is a great and terribly overlooked adventure, and a prism through which to view England during one of the most pivotal periods in its history. A Stain in the Blood is the story of a remarkable life, and of a journey that helped to shape a nation. It is a revelatory first work of non-fiction by one of the brightest young writers and thinkers of today

description: 223 pages : 22 cm

In Fifty Places to Paddle Before You Die, the newest addition to the Fifty Places series, Chris Santella explores the best destinations for the diverse sport of paddling. The book features the world's top spots for kayaking, rafting, canoeing, and stand-up paddleboarding. Destinations include the Grand Canyon, Alaska's Kenai Peninsula, Baja California, Indonesia's Komodo Islands, and the Antarctic Peninsula, as recommended by paddling experts. Compelling travelogues are complemented by beautiful and vibrant photographs of the locations and travel tips to help readers experience the destinations for themselves

selected.title: [Cicero (Ship) of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by John R. Stivers, keeper William. J. Chadwick and then Isaac Wrisley, on voyage 9 October 1860 - 25 May 1865],
selected.description: Logbook of a whaling voyage to the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic Oceans in addition ot the Sea of Okhotsk, the Yellow Sea, and the Sea of Japan. Includes descriptions of whales and walruses seen or taken, illnesses, accidents, deaths at sea, interactions with natives, desertions, a rescue, and punishments. Also contains illustrations of whales, pen and ink drawings of the rigging, a drawing of a clipper ship, profile views, oil shipped home, accounts of provisions, and a crew list. A heavy gale damaged the windlass on September 1, 1861. On 4 September 1861, the vessel took two men from the ship Emily Morgan who had originally belonged to the bark Alice Frazier when lost. One whale caught on 23 March 1862 was eaten by sharks before the crew was able to cut in. A Japanese war steamer took possession of the Bonin Islands on 5 April 1862 but the Cicero encountered no problems. Isaac Wrisley assumed logkeeping duties on 13 November 1862 after William Chadwick (First Mate) was fired for incompetence. One man died of consumption on December 28, 1862. The vessel took on a passenger to Guam in February 1863. The vessel was damaged by ice on July 17, 1863. The keeper reported that the vessel was leaking on October 11, 1863. The vessel was damaged by a typhoon on October 16, 1863. On 4 June 1864, the vessel encountered several starving people on McKean Island (Kiribati) and gave them some supplies. A sperm whale stove a whaleboat on June 14, 1864. The vessel took a passenger off the brig Kohala to the Sandwich Islands in August 1864. One man was sick with rheumatism on October 13, 1864. John Rotch fell overboard on 29 January 1865 but was saved. The Steward died on April 14, 1865. Other places represented include Cape Verde, Marquesas Islands, Maui, Bonin Islands, Honolulu, Saipan, Guam, and Lahaina. Whaling grounds include the Cape Verde, Coast of Brazil, Falkland Islands, Coast of Chile, Tuamotos, Japan, On the Line, Japan Sea, Okhotsk Sea, and the Bering Sea grounds.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 18); Whaling vessel out of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by John R. Stivers, on voyage 9 October 1860 - 25 May 1865; managing agent, Loum Snow; built in Rochester, Mass., 1823.

selected.title: Voyages from Montreal on the River St. Laurence, through the continent of North America, to the Frozen and Pacific Oceans, in the years 1789 and 1793: With a preliminary account of the rise, progress, and present state of the fur trade of that country
selected.description: Mackenzie, Alexander (Sir): 1763-1820. Born on island of Lewis; immigrated to New York then Montreal; entered service of Finlay, Gregory & Co., c. 1779; subsequently employed by Gregory, McLeod & Co. and NWC; in charge of Fort Chipewyan from 1788; retired to England, 1799; created knight bachelor, 1802; returned to Canada and fur trade, 1802-1808; cousin of Roderick Mackenzie (Wallace, Dictionary of Canadian biography ). // Combe, William: 1741-1823. Prolific English writer; assisted Alexander Mackenzie in preparation of Voyages , 1801 ( Dictionary of National Biography ). // Mackenzie, Roderick: d.1844. Fur trader; cousin of Sir Alexander Mackenzie; brother of Henry MacKenzie (Wallace, Dictionary of Canadian biography ). // After the preface there follow 132 pages on the history of the fur trade in the North West. Some authorities think this was written by his cousin, Roderick MacKenzie. According to the Dictionary of National Biography , Voyages , 1801, was compiled by William Combe from Mackenzie's notes. Includes vocabularies of the Knisteneaux, Algonquin, Chepewyan, Nagailer, and Atnah Indian languages. Errors in paging: page ix numbered xi; page 190 unnumbered; pages 212-216 numbered 214-218. Also published, 2nd edition, London: Printed for T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1801 ([2], cxxxii, viii, 412, [2]p.); including some material by Bougainville, London: Printed for T. Cadell, Jun. and W. Davies et al., 1802 (2 vols.); 1st American edition, New York: G.F. Hopkins, 1802 (viii [i.e. ix], 94, 296p.); 2nd American edition, Philadelphia: John Morgan, 1802 (viii, cxxvi, 392p.); 3rd American edition, New York: Evert Duyckinck, 1803 (viii, 437p.); edited by Richard Phillips and included in, A collection of voyages and travels, from the discovery of America to the commencement of the nineteeth [sic] century , vol.24, London: Printed for Richard Phillips, 1809 (392p.). New York: W.B. Gilley, 1814 (2 vols.); Toronto: George N. Morang, 1902 (2 vols.); with introduction by Robert Waite, New York: New Amsterdam Book Co., 1902 (2 vols.); New York: A.S. Barnes, 1903 (2 vols.); with introduction by W.L. Grant, Toronto: Courier Press, 1911 (2 vols.); New York: Allerton Book Co., 1922 (2 vols.), reprinted New York: AMS Press, 1973; with introduction by Charles William Colby and illustrations by C. Keith Gebhardt, Toronto: Radisson Society of Canada, 1927 (xxviii, 498p.); Ann Arbor, Mich.: University Microfilms, 1966 (cxxxii, viii, 412p.); [New York]: Readex Microprint Corp., 1966 (cxxxii, viii, 412p.); with introduction by Roy Daniells, Edmonton: M.G. Hurtig and Rutland, Vt.: Tuttle, 1971 (xx, cxxxii, 412p.). Also published as Alexander Mackenzie's voyage to the Pacific Ocean in 1793 , edited by Milo Milton Quaife, Chicago: Lakeside Press, 1931 (xxix, 384p.), reprinted, New York: Citadel Press, 1967 (xxix, 384p.). The 1789 journey also published in Exploring the Northwest Territory , edited by Ted Hayden McDonald, Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, [1966] (xiii, 133p.). The 1793 journey also published in First Man West: Alexander Mackenzie's journal of his voyage to the Pacific Coast of Canada in 1793 , edited by Walter Sheppe, Montreal: McGill University Press and Berkeley: University of California Press, 1962 (ix, 366p.), reprinted Westport Conn.: Greenwood Press, 1976 (ix, 366p.) and as Journal of the voyage to the Pacific , New York: Dover Publications, 1995 (ix, 366p.). Translated as Alexander Mackenzie's Esq. Reisen von Montreal durch Nordwestamerika nach dem Eismeer und der Sud-see in den Jahren 1789 und 1793: nebst einer Geschichte des Pelzhandels in Canada , Hamburg: B.G. Hoffmann, 1802 ([1], 1 leaf, [xiv], 585, [3]p.); translated by E.B. as Alexander Mackenzie's Esq. Reisen von Montreal durch Nordwestamerika nach dem Eismeer und der Sud-see in den Jahren 1789 und 1793? , Berlin: s.n., 1802 (408, [508]p.); translated and edited by Mathias Christian Sprengel as Alexander Mackenzie's Reise nach dem nördlichen Eisemeere vom 3. Jun bis 12. September 1798 , Weimar: Verlage des Landes-Industrie-Comptoirs, 1802 ([2], 61, [1]p.). For French version see Peel 54.

selected.title: [Milton (Ship) of New Bedford, mastered by Charles Halsey, keeper unknown, on voyage 6 September 1860 - 6 April 1865],
selected.description: Logbook of a whaling voyage to the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and the Okhotsk Sea. Includes descriptions of whales seen or taken, accidents, shipwrecks, and women on ships. Also contains whale stamps and anchor drawings. Crew boarded the abandonded bark Alice Frazier on 22 June 1861 in the Okhotsk Sea. In September 1862, the vessel dragged and just missed the Milo (Ship) in Shantar Bay. In June 1863, the vessel drifted into the ice and remained blocked in the ice for 50 days. Other places represented include Turtle Bay (Baja California, Mexico), Kahawai (Hawaii), Hope Island, Fabius Island and Rocky Point (Siberia), and Fabius Island (Nedorazumeniya Island). Whaling grounds include the San Antonio, Cornell, Coast of Brazil, Cape Horn, On the Line, Coast of Japan, East China Sea, Japan Sea, Okhotsk Sea, and the Coast of Califonria grounds.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 262); Whaling vessel, out of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Charles Halsey, on voyage 6 September 1860 - 6 Aprril 1865; managing agent: Henry Taber & Company ; built at Milton, Mass., 1815.

selected.title: [Zephyr (Ship) of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Abraham Gardner, keeper Michael Cumiskey, on voyage 29 June 1839 - 19 March 1843],
selected.description: Journal of a whaling voyage to the South Pacific and Indian Ocean. Includes descriptions of whales seen or taken, accidents at sea, illnesses, deaths at sea, punishment, and women onboard. Also contains a crew list, provisions, religious verses, and prayers. The ship lost 5 boats in the Indian Ocean as a result of a heavy gale. The crew received word of the murder of two missionaries by natives on February 10, 1840. On February 25, 1840, the steward attacked the captain and was punished. On April 25, 1840, while at Tahiti, one crewman "not being in his right mind" jumped overboard and drowned. The crew list is at the back of the book as well as a list of who raised whales. There are also numerous verses, prayers and references to the Scriptures. After seven months out the ship got its first whale. There were passengers from Oahu to New Bedford, including Reverend Dr. Lafon, his lady, and native servants. Dr. Lafon held church services every Sunday on the voyage home.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 306); Whaling vessel out of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Abraham Gardner, on voyage 29 June 1839 - 19 March 1893; managing agent, Alexander Gibbs; built in Middletown, Conn., 1815.

This is the log of a non-whaling vessel that travelled from New Bedford around Cape Horn to Honolulu and stayed there for six months. It then returned home after discharging unspecified cargo and coal, cleaning and painting the ship, and taking on board whale oil, some bone, hides, guano and 25 whalers. On December 1, 1864 the ship fired salutes to President Lincoln. It also had a very bad leak after a storm and discovered five feet of water in the hold.

selected.title: [Eagle (Ship) of Fairhaven, Mass., mastered by Samuel Perry, keeper Stephen Reed Delano, on voyage 18 December 1840 - 22 April 1843],
selected.description: Logbook of a whaling voyage to the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Includes descriptions of whales seen or taken, accidents, illnesses, desertions, punishments, and shipboard medicine. Also contains whale stamps, profile views, accounts, and a crew list. Three men were sick with scurvy on November 17, 1841. The ship landed at Maui and traded oil and flour for goats and pineapples on April 21, 1842. One man cut two of his toes off with a mincing knife on June 20, 1842. First mate Stephen R. Delano was left at Maui due to sickness on 26 August 1842, with the logbook being pooly kept as a result after this date. Whaling grounds include the Coast of Chile, Off Shore, Galapagos, On the Line, Coast of Brazil, and the 36/36 grounds.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 328); Whaling vessel out of Fairhaven, Mass., mastered by Samuel Perry, on voyage 18 December 1840 - 22 April 1843; managing agent, Hiram Henry Stackpole; built in Kennebunk, Maine.

selected.title: Logbook of the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass. Richard Mitchell (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., and Charles Carroll (Ship : 1832-1853) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Shubael Chase, Edy Coffin, Job C./E. Clark, and Josiah C. Long, kept by Josiah C. Long, on eight voyages from 24 June 1822-29 December 1852
selected.description: Logbook kept by Josiah C. Long comprised of eight whaling voyages. First voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Shubael Chase, from 24 June 1822 - 27 December 1824 to the Pacific Ocean Contains a long description of the Bounty mutiny and people on Pitcairn Island. The crew also witnessed a total solar eclipse on 26 June 1824. Second voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Edy Coffin, from 7 June 1825 - 16 October 1827 to the Brazil banks, South Pacific Ocean and coast of ChileDuring this voyage the ship saw 125 whales and caught 97. During a stop at the Juan Fernández Islands the ship was able to obtain peaches for the ship. There was one death at sea. Third voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Job C. Clark, from 19 April 1828 - 30 June 1829 to western and southern Atlantic Ocean for sperm and right whales [spelled "write"]. Fourth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Job E. Clark, from 15 November 1829 - 27 January 1833 to the Atlantic Ocean and Pacific Ocean sIn the company of several other vessel at times. Put into port at Rio de Janeiro for repairs. Fifth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 27 June 1833 - 16 November 1836 along Brazil and Chile and the South Pacific OceanDuring the voyage they saw 86 whales and caught 52. They spoke the Charles Carroll's captain Owen Chase who was a survivor of the Essex. Sixth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 1 September 1837 - 28 April 1841 to waters off Brazil, Chile, Peru and the South Pacific OceanThe ship encountered rough weather and could not reach the Azores. During the voyage nine men contracted smallpox. Seveth voyage documents the Richard Mitchell (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 14 October 1843 - 30 September 1847 to Brazil, Galapagos Islands, and the South Pacific OceanIncludes comments on the residents of Pitcairn Islands. It took the ship a month to round Cape Horn. Eighth voyage documents the Charles Carroll (Ship : 1832-1853) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 2 December 1848 - 29 December 1852 along the coast of Peru and the South Pacific Ocean. Voyage began by wrecking the rudder on an oil cask. Includes data on all vessels included in journal.

selected.title: [Huntress (Ship) of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Edward T. Shearman, keeper Stephen Devoll, on voyage 25 June 1844 - 27 May 1847],
selected.description: Logbook of a whaling voyage to the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans. Includes descriptions of whales seen or taken, accidents at sea, deaths at sea, mutinous behavior, interactions with natives, punishment on ships, and shipboard medicine. Also includes whale stamps, ships stamps, a crew list, and a list of provisions. The cooper broke his leg on 27 January 1845 and the captain set it. The ship came within six feet of fouling a ship in the night on January 22, 1847. George Shearman was killed by a whale on June 22, 1845. John Gomes fell from aloft and died on August 29, 1844.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 164); Whaling vessel out of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Edward T. Shearman, on voyage 25 June 1844 - 27 May 1847; managing agent, Robert Gibbs; built in Milton, Mass., 1811.

selected.title: [Cossack (Bark) of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Charles Slocum, keeper Benjamin Franklin Homan, on voyage 8 October 1850 - 10 May 1853],
selected.description: Logbook of a whaling voyage to the Atlantic, Pacific and, Arctic Oceans in addition to the Anadyr and Kamchatka Seas. Includes description of types of whales, seals, and walruses seen or taken, accidents, injuries, several deaths at sea, a fire on a ship, mutinous behavior, interactions with natives, punishments, a rescue at sea, and shipboard medicine. Also contains whale stamps, accounts, provisions used, and inventories of oil and bone. During the voyage the captain often disagreed with his charts. The keeper notes that there were 70-100 ships in the Arctic on 15 November 1852 and 100 ships (30 whalers) at Hong Kong on February 21 1852. The captain suffered an injury on December 24, 1850. While at Nauru [Pleasant Island] on 17 June 1852, the natives took the crew to the kings. The keeper records the death of Captain Joseph Bailey of the ship Champion on February 28, 1852. At one point, the vessel was damage in a gale. In 1852, the forecastle was smoked due to one of the crew dying of smallpox. Whaling grounds include the On the Line, Kamchatka, and the Arctic grounds.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 92); Whaling vessel out of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Charles Slocum, on voyage 8 October 1850 - 10 May 1853; managing agent, Charles Hitch; built in Nobleboro, Maine.

selected.title: Journal of the Mary Ann (Bark) and Chili (Bark)of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Alexander H. Macomber and Benjamin South Clark, keeper unknown, on two voyages from 9 May 1853-8 June 1860
selected.description: Journal, keeper unknown, comprised of two whaling voyages. First voyage documents the Mary Ann (Bark) of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Alexander H. Macomber, from 9 May 1853 - 20 May 1856 in the Atlantic Ocean. One month per page. Pages 1-7 contain poetry, pp. 8-16 blank. At one point there were 8 passengers aboard the ship. There was one death due to consumption. Second voyage documents the Chili (Bark) of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by Benjamin South Clark, from 31 July 1856 - 8 June 1860 to the Indian Ocean. Many ships were spoken/gammed during this voyage but there are very brief notes of other happenings.

Activities recorded include illnesses and accidents, taking on of recruits, assorted ship repairs, retrieving a cask full of sperm oil, hiring Maoris to hunt for deserters, finding women on the ship and having to chase them off the ship twice, and the keeper's nostalgia for the fourth of July at home.

selected.title: South from Ephesus : travels in Aegean Turkey
description: x, 266 p., [10] p. of plates : 20 cm

"Weary of what he called the 'tyranny' of Western art, Brian Sewell first visited Turkey--a country that had captivated him since he was a boy--in 1975. He thought that there, anything he found would have no relevance to the European art that he had so compulsively 'stitched into the dense fabric of my art-historical memory' and that he could therefore enjoy the art for its own sake. But Turkey surprised him and he delighted in the unexpected wealth of Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic cultures there, returning three of four times a year until 1990. The main bulk of this book focuses on his journey from Ephesus to Side one winter. With typically acerbic commentary, Sewell describes (not always favourably) the archaeological and historical sites he comes across, the landscapes that so clearly thrilled him, the encounters he has along the way and the fractious, though wonderfully funny, relationship he forms with Ayhan, his driver. South from Ephesus is an incomparable portrait of Turkey and its artistic heritage--a book that could only have been written by Sewell and which has become a quirky classic of travel literature"--Back cover

selected.title: DTIC ADA339268: Recursive Fitness
selected.description: The legendary scenario is chilling: A young man sails in the eastern Mediterranean or perhaps on the Aegean along with other members of an esoteric cult He is the only novice aboard; all the other voyagers are tried and true initiates. His brotherhood lives under arcane rules -- one may not eat beans, for instance -- and dedicates itself to discovering mathematical regularity in nature. The voyage affords time for reflection, and the young monk continues to work on a problem which has occupied him for several days. He scratches right triangles on a board and wonders: How can I show that the length of the hypotenuse can always be expressed as some relationship between two whole numbers.
